title: Dimensional and Spin Interpolation for the O$(n)$ Model: From Exact Anchors to RG-Improved Critical Exponents
abstract: We develop a two-axis interpolation framework for the O$(n)$ universality family, treating the spatial dimension $D$ and the spin-component number $n$ as independent continuous parameters connecting exact limiting solutions. On the spatial axis, anchoring between the Onsager solution at $D=2$ and mean-field theory at $D\to\infty$ yields a closed-form prediction for the 3D Ising critical coupling that agrees well with Monte Carlo benchmarks $K_c = 0.2204$ (benchmark: $0.22165$) with no adjustable parameters. Wilson--Fisher-constrained polynomial interpolation gives $ν=2/3$, $β=31/96$, and $η=35/864$ at $D=3$ (benchmarks: $0.6299$, $0.3265$, $0.0362$), and reproduces conformal-bootstrap results across $3 \le D < 4$. On the spin axis, we establish a necessary compatibility criterion: two-anchor interpolation succeeds only for observables that vary monotonically between the anchor values. The critical coupling $K_c(n)$ violates this criterion because the Heisenberg value falls below the spherical limit, whereas the correlation-length exponent $ν(n)$ satisfies it. A perturbative $1/n^2$ expansion yields $ν(3) = 0.7493$ (benchmark: $0.7112$), and propagation through exact scaling relations gives $β(3) = 0.3797$ (benchmark: $0.3689$) and $γ(3) = 1.489$ (benchmark: $1.396$), without introducing additional parameters. The framework naturally extends to non-integer spin, producing the prediction $ν(2.5) = 0.7143$ for the O$(2.5)$ universality class. These results establish dimensional and spin interpolation as a unified and predictive approach to critical phenomena, while clarifying the structural conditions under which interpolation succeeds.
summary: This paper presents a powerful two-axis interpolation framework to study critical behavior in the O(n) model by treating spatial dimension (D) and spin number (n) independently. By constraining polynomial fits using known exact limits, the authors achieve highly accurate predictions for critical exponents across various regimes. This work establishes a unified, predictive methodology for analyzing complex phase transitions.
main_problem: To develop a unified and predictive interpolation framework for critical phenomena across the O(n) universality family by treating both spatial dimension (D) and spin component number (n) as independent continuous parameters.
main_result:
The framework successfully predicts critical exponents like $
u(2.5)=0.7143$ and provides a highly accurate interpolation for $D=3$ using RG-improved polynomial fits, while also establishing structural compatibility criteria for the interpolation to be valid.
method: The authors employ two-axis interpolation techniques, connecting known exact limits (e.g., Onsager solution at D=2, Mean-Field theory at D->infinity) and utilizing Renormalization Group (RG) improved polynomial fitting constrained by known analytic structures.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the O(n) model, which generalizes the Ising model to spins with n components. The analysis is applied to critical phenomena in various dimensions ($D$) and spin values ($n$), including quantum-classical mappings for the Transverse Field Ising Model (TFIM).
key_observables:
Critical exponents ($
u,  eta, \eta, \gamma$) and the critical coupling constant ($K_c$).
important_parameters: Spatial dimension $D$, spin component number $n$, and the reduced temperature/coupling parameter $\epsilon = 4-D$.
main_assumptions: The interpolation requires that observables vary monotonically between the chosen anchor points; furthermore, the derivation of scaling relations relies on hyperscaling hypotheses valid below the upper critical dimension ($d_c=4$).
figures_summary:
Figures illustrate the comparison of interpolated exponents ($
u,  eta, \eta$) versus $D$, comparing linear interpolation against RG-improved results and exact anchor values.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes dimensional interpolation using two anchors (Onsager/Mean-Field) for the D-axis. It then develops spin interpolation along the n-axis, deriving necessary compatibility criteria. Finally, it unifies these concepts to create a predictive framework applicable across both axes simultaneously.
why_interesting: While focused on classical critical phenomena, the rigorous mathematical machinery of parameter-free interpolation and RG constraints is highly relevant for understanding quantum phase transitions in many-body systems where dimensionality or interaction strength can be treated as continuous parameters.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. RG-improved spatial interpolation for ν, β, η of the Ising (n = 1) universality class as functions of D ∈[2, 4]. Dashed blue: linear interpolation in δD = 1/(D −1). Solid red: RG-improved polynomials (22), (23), (24). Filled circles: exact anchor values (D = 2: Onsager/Yang [7, 13]; D = 4: mean-field [14]). Open circles: accepted values at D = 3 [9, 10]. Diamonds: RG-improved predictions at D = 3.

FIG. 2. The (n, D) parameter space for the O(n) model. Four colored markers: exact-anchor corners (Onsager [7], mean-field [14], Mermin–Wagner [21], Berlin–Kac spherical [11]). Gray markers: physical targets at D = 3 (Ising, XY, Heisenberg). Blue arrow: spatial (D-axis) interpolation direction. Red arrow: spin (n-axis) interpolation direction.

FIG. 3. Critical coupling Kc(n) at D = 3 on the simple-cubic lattice. Filled circles: Monte Carlo values [9, 23, 24]. Diamond: exact spherical limit K(sph) c = W3/4 ≈0.12636 [11, 20]. Dashed blue: zeroth-order affine interpolation (36). Solid red: first- order perturbative 1/n2 formula (39). The shaded region marks Kc(n) < K(sph) c , demonstrating the non-monotone structure that violates Proposition 1.

FIG. 4. Correlation-length exponent ν(n) at D = 3. Filled circles: accepted values [9, 10, 23, 24]; diamond: exact spherical limit ν(sph) = 1 [22]. Dashed blue: zeroth-order bivariate formula ν(0) = 1 −1/(3n) (59). Solid red: first-order perturbative formula (49). The perturbative result reduces the Heisenberg error from 25% to 5.4%.
